_design: MIRROR PAIRS. Each pair (a/b) shares the IDENTICAL four options verbatim; only the audio differs, and it selects a different key. Any strategy that reads only the options must therefore score 25% across the set by construction — there is no 'most complete', 'most hedged', or 'most specific' option, because every option is the key in some item. This is the falsifiable version of 'distractors must not be mutations of the key': if a blind solver still beats chance here, the leak is NOT in the option set and re-authoring distractors cannot fix the bank.

items.audio: STUDENT: I wanted to ask about the field trip fee. PROFESSOR: It's forty dollars, due Friday. STUDENT: That's the problem — I don't get paid until the fifteenth. PROFESSOR: Then talk to the department office. They keep a small fund for exactly this, and they can cover it and let you repay later in the term. It's not a scholarship, it's a loan, so you'd still owe it. STUDENT: But I would be able to go. PROFESSOR: You would.
items.stem: What does the professor suggest the student do?

options.A: Ask the department office about a fund that covers the fee up front
options.B: Skip the trip and complete an alternative written assignment
options.C: Pay a reduced fee because of documented financial hardship
options.D: Request that the payment deadline be moved to after the fifteenth

items.audio: So the puzzle with these desert beetles is where the water comes from. There's no standing water for months. What they do is stand facing the morning fog with the back tilted up. The shell has bumps that the fog condenses onto, and channels between them that run the droplets down to the mouth. They are not drinking dew off plants and they are not making water metabolically — they are harvesting it directly out of moving air.
items.stem: According to the lecture, how do the beetles obtain water?

options.A: By producing it internally as a by-product of metabolism
options.B: By condensing fog on the body and channelling it to the mouth
options.C: By absorbing dew that collects on desert vegetation overnight
options.D: By extracting moisture from the tissues of the insects they eat

items.audio: Now, the fog-harvesting beetle is famous, but it's the exception. Most beetles in this desert never touch free water at all. They're predators, and their prey is mostly water by mass. A beetle eating soft-bodied larvae takes in everything it needs that way, which is why you find them active in the driest months when there is no fog at all on the coast. The fog specialists are a coastal minority.

items.audio: The collapse of that trading city has been blamed on everything, but the sediment cores settle it. You see a sharp drop in river silt about a decade before the city empties. The river had shifted course upstream. Without the river the harbour silted shut, and a port city with no port is just an inland town with too many warehouses. The population left over about fifteen years. No siege layer, no ash, no mass graves.
items.stem: What does the professor identify as the cause of the city's decline?

options.A: A military conquest that destroyed the city's defensive walls
options.B: An epidemic that sharply reduced the working population
options.C: A shift in the river that closed the city's harbour
options.D: A change in trade routes that bypassed the region entirely

items.audio: People assume the harbour silting is what killed that city, but the silting happened two centuries earlier and the city carried on fine — they dredged. What actually ends it is the northern overland route opening. Once caravans could cross the mountains directly, nobody needed to come down to the coast at all. The warehouse records show goods volume falling while the population is still stable, which is the signature of a place being routed around rather than emptied out.

items.audio: What makes this pigment unusual is stability. Most organic reds fade badly in sunlight — a few decades and you have brown. This one is bound to a clay substrate, and the clay's lattice physically holds the dye molecule in a position where the light-driven reaction can't proceed. Same dye, unbound, fades in a season. It's not a more robust molecule; it's a molecule that has been immobilised.
items.stem: Why does the professor say this pigment resists fading?

options.A: The dye molecule is chemically more stable than similar reds
options.B: A clay substrate holds the molecule so the reaction cannot occur
options.C: A surface varnish blocks ultraviolet light from reaching it
options.D: The pigment is applied in layers thick enough to mask any change

items.audio: The clay-binding story is the one in the textbooks and it's been overtaken. Researchers made the pigment without any clay at all and it held up identically. What's actually going on is the varnish these workshops used over the top — a resin layer that absorbs almost everything in the ultraviolet. Strip the varnish and the same clay-bound pigment fades on schedule. The protection was never in the pigment. It was sitting on top of it.
items.stem: Why does the professor say this pigment resists fading?

options.A: The dye molecule is chemically more stable than similar reds
options.B: A clay substrate holds the molecule so the reaction cannot occur
options.C: A surface varnish blocks ultraviolet light from reaching it
options.D: The pigment is applied in layers thick enough to mask any change

items.audio: The surprise in the tree-ring record is the timing. Everyone expected the growth collapse to line up with the drought years, and it doesn't — the rings are narrow starting three years BEFORE the drought begins. What that tells us is that the trees were already stressed, almost certainly by the insect outbreak documented in the same period. The drought finished off a forest that was going anyway.
items.stem: What does the tree-ring evidence indicate?

options.A: The forest was already weakened by insects before the drought
options.B: The drought was more severe than written records suggested
options.C: Growth recovered faster than expected once rainfall returned
options.D: The trees were cut for timber rather than dying naturally

items.audio: The rings line up with the drought exactly — no lead, no lag — but they're far narrower than the rainfall figures in the monastery records would predict. Those records were kept for tax purposes and they systematically understate a bad year, because a bad year meant relief payments. The trees are the honest witness here, and they say the drought was considerably worse than the paperwork admits.
items.stem: What does the tree-ring evidence indicate?

options.A: The forest was already weakened by insects before the drought
options.B: The drought was more severe than written records suggested
options.C: Growth recovered faster than expected once rainfall returned
options.D: The trees were cut for timber rather than dying naturally

items.audio: The reason these seeds germinate only after fire isn't the heat, which is what people assume. You can heat them in an oven to the same temperature and nothing happens. It's a compound in the smoke — one specific molecule in the smoke of burning vegetation that the seed coat responds to. You can dissolve it in water and water the seeds with it, no fire involved, and they come up.
items.stem: What triggers germination in these seeds?

options.A: The high temperature reached during a fire
options.B: A chemical compound present in vegetation smoke
options.C: The removal of competing plants from the surrounding soil
options.D: The increase in soil nutrients from deposited ash

items.audio: The smoke-chemical mechanism is real in other species but not this one — smoke water does nothing here. What these seeds are responding to is light. They sit under a dense canopy of shrubs, and germination is suppressed until that canopy goes. Fire is simply the usual way it goes. Clear the same plot by hand, no fire, no smoke, and you get the identical flush of seedlings the following spring.
items.stem: What triggers germination in these seeds?

options.A: The high temperature reached during a fire
options.B: A chemical compound present in vegetation smoke
options.C: The removal of competing plants from the surrounding soil
options.D: The increase in soil nutrients from deposited ash
